editorial_contributions.text: The paper improves on the upper bound for the upper density of sets avoiding two points at unit distance apart in Euclidean spaces, both asymptotically, and numerically for dimensions between 4 and 24. The results depend on the study of an analogue of Lovász' \(\vartheta\) function for the (infinite) unit distance graph and on some finite subgraphs of the unit distance graph. As a consequence, improved lower bounds are obtained for the measurable chromatic number of the Euclidean space for dimensions between 4 and 24.

editorial_contributions.text:
Under the title ``Fundamentals of Classic and Modern Error-Correcting Codes'' the authors have taken the Sisyphus task of introducing to the reader the vast fields of coding theory and how error-correcting codes (ECCs) can be used to achieve reliable communications and data storage. The main topic of this book is focused on ECCs with block structure (block codes) and their contemporary developments in construction, encoding, and decoding techniques.

These ever evolving topics are summarized in seventeen chapters and five appendices. In my opinion the authors excel in they claim effort to convey to the readers the beauty and usefulness of ECCs and entice him ``... to follow and fully understand the topic with a minimum barrier.'' To this end long derivations and excessive proofs are avoided and each chapter concludes with twenty to fifty references for books and journal papers pointing the reader to the rigorous proofs and additional information on the topic.

The book truly explains these highly mathematical subjects to a level that can be accessed and applied with as little background in mathematics as possible. It provides step-by-step explanation of all covered topics, both more theoretical or applied, and includes sufficient illustrative examples to assist understanding. After familiarizing the reader to the topic of each chapter more than 300 challenging homework problems (except for the introductory first chapter) are included to strengthen the comprehension of the material. Like all great math books a solutions manual of all problems is available online for instructors.

The book begins with an introduction on the main problem of coding for reliable digital transmission and storage of information. The main topics in the first chapter are categories of codes, modulation/demodulation, hard- and soft-decision, maximum aposteriori and maximum likelihood decoding. More information is given on channel capacity, classification of channel errors, error-control strategies and measures of code performance.

Chapter 2 presents some important elements of algebra (groups, finite fields, polynomials, vector spaces over finite fields, matrices) and graphs necessary for understanding the rest of the chapters of the book. Chapter 3 gives an introduction to linear block codes, generator and parity-check matrices, minimum distance and general and minimum-distance decoding. Chapter 4 focuses on cyclic codes that are crucial for most error-correcting schemes. Aside from cyclic code and their encoding/decoding the class of quasicyclic codes (QC) is described.

The next two chapters (Chapters 5 and 6) cover the binary BCH, and nonbinary BCH codes, respectively. Special attention is devoted to the class of Reed-Solomon (RS) codes.

Chapter 7 presents the finite-geometry codes that are interesting because of their distinctive geometric structures allowing them to be decoded with various decoding methods.

The eight chapter considers the Reed-Muller (RM) codes and their use for correcting multiple random errors. Using a geometric approach, RM codes can be put in cyclic form forming a special subclass of finite-geometry codes.

The next chapter nine is an auxiliary presentation of some coding techniques like interleaving, direct product, concatenation, turbo coding, \((u \vert u + v)\)-construction and Kronecker product. Lastly in this chapter the ARQ and HARQ schemes that provide highly reliable information transmission in two-way communication systems are covered.

Chapter 10 studies codes and coding techniques that are effective for correcting bursts of errors, random erasures, and bursts of erasures.

Chapter 11 introduces low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes which can achieve near Shannon limit performance on various communication and data-storage channels. LDPC are currently considered standard codes for various current and next-generation communication systems, such as wireless (4G, 5G, etc.), optical, satellite, space, digital video broadcast among others. The chapter covers the basic concepts and definitions, matrix and graph representations, and original construction methods for LDPC codes as well as their decoding and error performance.

Chapter 12 presents the class of finite-geometry (FG) LDPC codes which are constructed based on finite geometries and are the only class of LDPC codes with cyclic structure.

Chapter 13 considers a class of LDPC codes constructed based on partial geometries (PaGs). The coverage of this chapter includes construction of PaGs (and their associated QC-LDPC codes) based on: cyclic subgroups of prime order of finite fields; prime fields; and a special class of designs, called balanced incomplete block designs.

Next two chapters (14 and 15) are devoted to the construction of QC-LDPC codes based on finite, and LDPC codes constructed using graphs, respectively. In Chapter 15, two graphical methods to construct LDPC codes are presented resulting in so-called graph-theoretic LDPC codes.

Chapter 16 focuses on a universal coding scheme for collective encoding/decoding and iterative soft-decision decoding of cyclic codes of prime lengths. The coverage of this chapter includes: cyclic code of prime length; code composition, cascading, and interleaving of codewords in a cyclic code of prime length; GFT of an interleaved and cascaded composite code and much more.

The last Chapter 17 presents the class of polar codes which approach channel capacity. Their construction, encoding, and decoding are masterfully described.
